\title{Calibrated Escalation for IT Ticket Triage:\\
What the Calibration Distribution Decides}

\begin{abstract}
An IT ticket triage system has to route a ticket to the right team, and it also has to recognise when it should not answer and hand the ticket to a person. We build a triage pipeline around that second requirement. It has two independently calibrated escalation gates: a confidence threshold on a lexical first-tier classifier, and a similarity threshold on retrieval that decides whether a language model may draft a resolution grounded in past tickets. A zero-shot LLM classifies more accurately than our trained classifier, but it has no abstention guarantee, no calibrated gate and no cost model; that contrast is the argument of the paper. Across coverage guarantees, drift monitoring and classification, one result recurs: the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint. We also report what did not work. The two-tier cascade is a latency optimisation, not an accuracy gain; a retrieval-sufficiency check catches both unsupported drafts and is still not usable as a gate; and an LLM judge agreed with human labels at a chance-level Cohen's $\kappa$. Every number is regenerated from a committed result file.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
ticket triage, selective prediction, conformal prediction, retrieval-augmented generation, escalation, reproducibility
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ===========================================================================
Support tickets arrive as free text written by people who do not know which team owns their problem. A triage system that routes a ticket confidently and wrongly costs more than one that asks for help: the ticket waits in the wrong queue, and an automatically drafted fix may be applied to the wrong problem. The design question is therefore not only how accurate the system is, but when it declines to answer.

We treat escalation to a human as the primary output of a triage pipeline. Our pipeline classifies a ticket into one of \nb{T19.categories} teams with a two-tier cascade, retrieves similar resolved tickets, and allows a language model to draft a resolution only when retrieval clears a calibrated similarity threshold. Each threshold was set by measurement and is recorded with its evidence (Section~\ref{sec:method}).

The obvious objection is that a large language model can simply classify the ticket. It can: on our out-of-template benchmark a zero-shot model is more accurate than our trained classifier (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). But it offers no abstention guarantee, no calibrated gate and no cost model, and it is the gate, not the accuracy, that decides whether a wrong answer reaches a user. We report that baseline prominently because the contrast is the argument.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A calibrated two-gate escalation pipeline} whose thresholds are independently calibrated and re-calibratable, with the evidence behind each, including the attempts that failed.
\item \textbf{A cross-phase finding}: the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint. It holds for a coverage guarantee and a drift reference, and for a trained classifier.
\item \textbf{Honest baselines}: a controlled ablation showing the cascade buys latency rather than accuracy, zero-shot LLM baselines from two vendors, an audited LLM judge that fails silently, and a retrieval-sufficiency gate that fails for a reason we can name.
\end{enumerate}
Every number is emitted from a committed result file, and the audit method that found and corrected several of our own published figures is in the supplement.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Ticket triage.} Automated routing and escalation of IT and support tickets has been studied with LLM-based methods~\cite{tickit,paket_ticket,redcap_llm_triage}.
These works mostly report routing accuracy; our focus is the abstention decision around the classifier.

\textbf{Cascades and deferral.} Confidence-based cascades defer inputs from a cheap model to an expensive one~\cite{jitkrittum_cascade}. Conformal variants give distribution-free accuracy guarantees for multi-tier cascades~\cite{conformal_cascade}, and cascades can end in a human decision-maker~\cite{fanconi_defer}.
We compare deferral rules at the coverage the live gate actually runs at.

\textbf{Conformal prediction under shift.} Split conformal prediction gives marginal coverage under exchangeability~\cite{vovk_alrw,angelopoulos_gentle}, weighted conformal prediction restores it under covariate shift given the likelihood ratio~\cite{tibshirani_covshift}, and later work bounds the loss beyond exchangeability~\cite{barber_beyond} and adapts online~\cite{gibbs_adaptive}. Our coverage measurements are an empirical instance of that gap, on text whose shift is a change of register.

\textbf{Abstention in retrieval-augmented generation.} Retrieval-augmented generation~\cite{lewis_rag} can be gated on whether the retrieved context suffices~\cite{joren_sufficient} or corrected when retrieval is poor~\cite{crag}.
We test a sufficiency rater as a second gate.

\textbf{LLM judges.} Jung et al.~\cite{jung_trust_escalate} propose judges with guarantees of human agreement that escalate when unsure, and Jain et al.~\cite{jain_judges} address an agreeableness bias in judge evaluations.
Our judge shows the failure these works caution against.

\textbf{Synthetic benchmarks.} The efficacy of synthetic data as an evaluation benchmark has itself been studied~\cite{maheshwari_synthetic}.
We treat what our synthetic corpus can and cannot measure as a result.

\textbf{Positioning.} Table~\ref{tab:related} compares our pipeline with the closest of these works, using only what each abstract states. Two ticket-triage works evaluate on real tickets and we do not (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}); none describes escalation gates calibrated on measured evidence that allow generation only when retrieval clears them.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Methodology}
\label{sec:method}
% ===========================================================================
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the pipeline: a sequential pipeline with agent boundaries and an HTTP surface, not a distributed or autonomous multi-agent system. Each stage (classify, retrieve, resolve) is an agent that declares the artifacts it depends on, is checked for them when it is constructed, and decides nothing. Every routing decision lives in one orchestrator, which records a trace per stage, including the stages it deliberately skipped, so a skipped resolution step is positive evidence that no language model was called. The stages are individually addressable over HTTP, but the triage endpoint orchestrates in-process, so the measured path has no network hops. A stage failure becomes an escalation envelope rather than a server error, because the ticket then needs a human rather than a retry.

\textbf{Classification cascade.} Tier-1 is TF-IDF with logistic regression, fitted against a committed vocabulary so that its features are the same on every machine. If its top-class probability is at least \nb{F1.gate.cascade@r2}, its label stands. Otherwise Tier-2 answers: logistic regression over frozen BGE embeddings~\cite{bge} (bge-base-en-v1.5, \nb{T18.embedding_dim} dimensions). The threshold was calibrated on paraphrased tickets rather than on an in-distribution split, where every confidence bucket sits at the accuracy ceiling (Section~\ref{sec:gates}).

\textbf{Retrieval gate and grounded drafting.} The ticket's top-\nb{T19.rag_top_k} neighbours are retrieved from a FAISS inner-product index~\cite{faiss} over resolved tickets. If the top-1 cosine similarity is below \nb{F1.gate.rag@r2}, the ticket is escalated and no language model is called. Above it, Gemini (gemini-flash-lite) drafts a resolution from the retrieved tickets. Its prompt carries each neighbour's title, description, resolution, category and similarity, tells it to base every step only on those past fixes rather than on outside knowledge, and tells it to say so and recommend a human check when the examples do not match. The language model never decides the category. The retrieval threshold was chosen on a combined set of in-domain and out-of-domain tickets and checked against an adversarial set (Section~\ref{sec:gates}).

\textbf{Independence of the gates.} The cascade threshold depends only on Tier-1's confidence, so swapping the Tier-2 embedding model does not require recalibrating it. The retrieval threshold is specific to the embedding model and must be recalibrated on any model swap.

\textbf{Conformal measurement.} To ask whether a finite-sample guarantee could replace the cascade threshold, we calibrate split conformal prediction~\cite{vovk_alrw,angelopoulos_gentle} for each tier. A nonconformity score is computed from the classifier's predicted probabilities on a held-out calibration set, and its empirical quantile fixes a prediction set whose marginal miscoverage is at most $\alpha$ when calibration and test tickets are exchangeable. This is measurement only: it runs offline and gates nothing in production. Section~\ref{sec:finding1} tests whether the guarantee survives the move from calibration to out-of-template text.

\textbf{Automation candidates.} An offline path clusters resolved tickets by the similarity of their resolution text at \nb{F1.gate.clustering@r2} and surfaces recurring clusters to a human reviewer as candidates for automation.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Origin of the corpus.} The project follows a nasscom hackathon use-case brief, which specified the \nb{T19.categories} categories, routing, resolution suggestion, confidence-based escalation and automation flagging, and explicitly recommended a synthetic, LLM-generated dataset with title, description, category, resolution and priority fields. We followed it at \nb{T19.dataset_rows} rows. The synthetic corpus is a followed specification, not a convenience substitute for real tickets.

\textbf{The corpus as an object of study.} Three measurements say what it is worth. \emph{The templates are the fix classes}, so clustering precision cannot be measured on it; this is a related dataset limitation, not an instance of Section~\ref{sec:named}. \emph{Memorisation is template-level}: our calibration set touches \nb{T8.templates_touched} of \nb{T8.templates_total} templates, and removing whole templates would leave \nb{T8.rows_surviving_template_exclusion} of \nb{T8.dataset_rows} rows, so it cannot be de-contaminated by filtering. \emph{Training rows buy little off-template} (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). Details are in the supplement, \emph{Corpus and evaluation sets}.

\textbf{Evaluation sets.} In-distribution accuracy is uninformative on template-generated data: the TF-IDF baseline scores \nb{T1.tfidf_baseline.in_distribution_accuracy@pct0}\% on a held-out split, which we treat as a warning. We evaluate on three fixed, read-only sets written outside the templates: a hand-written \nb{T19.benchmark14.n}-ticket benchmark, a \nb{T19.benchmark45.n}-ticket out-of-template benchmark, and a \nb{T19.adversarial.n}-ticket adversarial set (off-topic, vague and slang tickets, each with an expected escalate-or-proceed outcome). A \nb{T19.deployment175.n}-ticket deployment-distribution set, in the benchmark's register rather than the templates', is a second calibration and evaluation distribution. The benchmark and the deployment set were generated with Gemini.

\textbf{Statistics.} Proportions carry a Wilson 95\% interval~\cite{wilson}; paired comparisons use the exact McNemar test~\cite{mcnemar}. A difference smaller than its own noise band is never written as an ordered comparison.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
% ===========================================================================
\subsection{The escalation gates}
\label{sec:gates}
\textbf{Retrieval gate.} Table~\ref{tab:gates} gives both gates at their live operating points. The retrieval threshold was chosen on a combined set of in-domain and out-of-domain tickets. At \nb{T5.gate@r2}, all \nb{T5.in_domain_proceed_at_gate} in-domain tickets proceed and \nb{T5.ood_leakage_at_gate@pct1}\% of out-of-domain tickets leak through; two steps lower, leakage nearly triples to \nb{T5.ood_leakage_below_gate@pct1}\%. The threshold also sits inside the adversarial safe range [\nb{T5.safe_range_low@r4}, \nb{T5.safe_range_high@r4}], from the highest similarity among tickets that must escalate to the lowest among tickets that must proceed. With the gate, the pipeline decides \nb{T3.baseline.escalation_correct} adversarial tickets correctly; with it removed, \nb{T3.norag.escalation_correct}. The gate errs in both directions: benchmark tickets \nb{T17.G021.ticket} and \nb{T17.G024.ticket} cleared it and drew drafts a human labelled ungrounded, and \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.ticket} was escalated although its context was adequate. One similarity threshold is the simplest rule that works on this corpus, not a claim that one scalar suffices (supplement, \emph{Retrieval gate}).

\textbf{Cascade threshold.} Of \nb{T4.calibration.attempts_total} calibration attempts, two were rejected: an in-distribution split, where every confidence bucket sits at the accuracy ceiling, and a small hand-written set that was never committed. The third, on paraphrased tickets, returns \nb{T4.sweep.threshold.target80@r2}, the live gate, at the two looser target accuracies (supplement, \emph{Cascade calibration and in-distribution reliability}). The in-distribution reliability figures are a ceiling effect: observed accuracy is \nb{T4.observed_accuracy_every_bin@r1} in every bin, so both tiers are under-confident there (ECE \nb{T4.tier1.ece@r3} and \nb{T4.tier2.ece@r3}).

\subsection{Coverage transfer and the calibration distribution}
\label{sec:finding1}
We calibrate split conformal prediction for both tiers on \nb{T10.deployment.n_calibration} tickets and evaluate coverage on the out-of-template benchmark (Fig.~\ref{fig:coverage}, Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t7_t10_coverage}).

\textbf{Finding~1, in three clauses that must be read together.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Measured on our corpus}, split-conformal coverage transfers for the BGE representation but not the lexical one. At $\alpha=\nb{T7.alpha@r2}$ Tier-1's coverage gap is \nb{T7.tier1.coverage_gap@r3} and Tier-2's is \nb{T7.tier2.coverage_gap@r3}, against a noise band of $\pm$\nb{T7.noise_band_2sd@r3} (two standard deviations over the calibration draw).
\item \emph{External replication is inconclusive.} On an external corpus that is independently generated, not real production data, a version shift left the tiers indistinguishable (\nb{T11.7b.tier1.coverage_gap@r4} against \nb{T11.7b.tier2.coverage_gap@r4}, band $\pm$\nb{T11.7b.noise_band_2sd@r4}); a version shift is the wrong type for a surface-vocabulary mechanism, and that corpus has almost no representation gap (label accuracy \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier1@pct1}\% against \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier2@pct1}\%). A paraphrase shift, the right type, was blocked by its own pre-registered degeneracy rule at a domain AUC of \nb{T11.7c.tfidf_domain_auc@r4}. Finding~1 has been shown neither to hold nor to fail outside its original corpus (supplement, \emph{External validity}).
\item \emph{Post-hoc evidence of the mechanism appears in accuracy.} Under the paraphrase shift Tier-1 lost \nb{T11.7c.accuracy.tier1_change@abs@pct1} accuracy points against Tier-2's \nb{T11.7c.accuracy.tier2_change@abs@pct1}; the difference-in-differences is \nb{T11.7c.did_point}. This is post-hoc and does not replace the blocked primary.
\end{itemize}

\input{tables/ieee/T7_T10_coverage.tex}

\textbf{The calibration distribution.} Recalibrating on the deployment-distribution set, with the same method, $\alpha$ and benchmark, moves Tier-1's gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3}. Only the calibration distribution changed. Distribution matching is necessary but not sufficient, since the residual stays well outside the band; for Tier-2 the payoff is set size. Covariate reweighting with a density ratio~\cite{tibshirani_covshift} is likewise a partial repair, not a correction (supplement, \emph{Weighted conformal under shift}). For the pipeline this means the lexical tier's guarantee cannot be quoted on out-of-template text, which is one reason conformal prediction stays a measurement rather than a gate.

\subsection{The cascade buys latency, not accuracy}
\label{sec:ablation}
Letting Tier-1 answer everything (\nb{T1.tier1only.benchmark45@frac}) is \nb{T3.repr_gap_points@r1} points below the full pipeline, but that is the gap between the BGE and TF-IDF representations, not the value of cascading. The control that isolates the cascade is Tier-2 answering everything (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t3_compact}). Against it the cascade is one ticket worse on each set: \nb{T3.cascade_delta.benchmark45} on the benchmark (\nb{T1.cascade.benchmark45@frac} against \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac}, exact McNemar $p=\nb{T3.mcnemar.benchmark45@r3}$) and \nb{T3.cascade_delta.deployment175} on the deployment set (\nb{T1.cascade.deployment175@frac} against \nb{T1.tier2only.deployment175@frac}, $p=\nb{T3.mcnemar.deployment175@r3}$). What it buys is latency: Tier-2 costs \nb{T3.latency.tier2_over_tier1@r1}$\times$ Tier-1 (\nb{T3.latency.tier2_median_ms@r1} against \nb{T3.latency.tier1_median_ms@r2}\,ms median), so the cascade saves \nb{T3.latency.saving.benchmark45@pct0}\% of median per-ticket latency on the benchmark and \nb{T3.latency.saving.deployment175@pct0}\% on the deployment set. The saving is larger on the deployment set because more of its tickets clear the Tier-1 threshold and never reach the encoder.

\input{tables/ieee/T3_compact.tex}

\subsection{Zero-shot LLM baselines}
\label{sec:zeroshot}
Two zero-shot LLMs received byte-identical prompts: Gemini (gemini-flash-lite) and Qwen2.5-3B, a 3B-parameter open-weight model run locally on a laptop CPU~\cite{qwen25}. Fig.~\ref{fig:accuracy} places them beside every classifier we measured on the benchmark. A 3B model on a laptop CPU, with no training on this corpus, is not beaten by a classifier fitted on \nb{T19.train_rows} of its rows, and this holds across two vendors. The readings differ by pair and are not merged:
\begin{itemize}
\item Gemini scores \nb{T1.zeroshot_gemini.benchmark45@frac} (95\% CI \nb{T1.zeroshot_gemini.benchmark45@ci}) and is distinguishably better than Tier-2's \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac} ($p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.gemini_vs_tier2.benchmark45@r3}$).
\item Qwen2.5-3B scores \nb{T1.zeroshot_qwen.benchmark45@frac} (95\% CI \nb{T1.zeroshot_qwen.benchmark45@ci}) and is indistinguishable from Tier-2 ($p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.qwen_vs_tier2.benchmark45@r3}$). Indistinguishable is not better.
\item Qwen2.5-3B against Gemini gives $p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.qwen_vs_gemini.benchmark45@r3}$, which is not significant.
\end{itemize}
The benchmark was generated with Gemini, so the Qwen arm is the partial control for authorship, and Gemini's extra margin cannot be attributed to capability rather than authorship. This is a zero-shot LLM against a trained classifier, which is not like-for-like: it measures what a template-generated training corpus is worth on out-of-template phrasing, not whether a language model outperforms the pipeline as a system, whose contribution is the calibrated escalation neither zero-shot model provides. Infrastructure recall is \nb{T2.gemini.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for Gemini, \nb{T2.qwen.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for Qwen and \nb{T2.tier2.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for the trained classifier, which points at the tickets rather than the methods (supplement, \emph{Zero-shot baselines in detail}).

Among the trained classifiers, the choice of representation matters more than the choice of model family. The lexical tier alone scores \nb{T1.tier1only.benchmark45@frac}, two other frozen sentence encoders with the same logistic head score \nb{T1.minilm.benchmark45@frac} and \nb{T1.e5.benchmark45@frac}, and a fine-tuned DistilBERT scores \nb{T1.distilbert.benchmark45@frac} and \nb{T1.distilbert.reference.benchmark45@frac} in two runs of one configuration. Those two runs differ, so we draw no ordering between them, and neither approaches the frozen BGE encoder.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering

\subsection{Groundedness, an LLM judge, and a sufficiency gate}
\label{sec:grounded}
Every benchmark and adversarial ticket that clears the retrieval gate (\nb{T15.population.eligible} tickets) received a draft, and a human labelled \nb{T14.grounded@frac} of them grounded in the retrieved text (95\% CI \nb{T14.grounded@ci}). An LLM judge on the same rubric agreed with those labels on \nb{T14.judge.raw_agreement} drafts yet reached Cohen's $\kappa=\nb{T14.judge.cohens_kappa@r3}$~\cite{cohen_kappa}, because every disagreement was the judge substituting appropriateness for support; we treat a judge as an object of study, never as an unaudited scaling tool. A retrieval-sufficiency rater that never sees a draft caught \nb{T15.caught_of_ungrounded} of the ungrounded drafts but also flagged \nb{T15.flagged_of_grounded@frac} of the grounded ones, and the scalar gate errs the other way on \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.ticket}, so the rater is not usable as a gate (supplement, \emph{Groundedness, the judge and sufficiency}).

\subsection{The named finding}
\label{sec:named}
\textbf{The data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint.} It has two scoped instance classes. \emph{Calibration and reference distributions}: recalibrating on a deployment-distribution set moved Tier-1's coverage gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3} with nothing else changed (Section~\ref{sec:finding1}); and legitimate deployment-register tickets flag against the in-domain drift reference at \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.flag_rate.alpha0.01@r3} to \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.flag_rate.alpha0.2@r3} across four $\alpha$ levels, \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.ratio_to_null.min@r1} to \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.ratio_to_null.max@r1} times the per-ticket null, so a monitor on that reference would alarm continuously whatever the test, $\alpha$ or window (supplement, \emph{Drift detection}). \emph{Training distribution}: training on the corpus does not carry to out-of-template phrasing better than no training at all (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). The template redundancy of Section~\ref{sec:setup} and the sufficiency result are related findings, not instances.

\textbf{Methodological lessons.} An area-under-the-risk--coverage metric returned effects the pre-registered comparison at the live gate's operating coverage could not resolve, so an averaged metric is never a reason to promote a deferral rule. A pre-registered degeneracy rule blocked our paraphrase-shift experiment, and we did not revise it after seeing the results even though a critique of it was sound. Nine times, a value or artifact was wrong for its context yet internally consistent and produced a wrong result silently; each is documented in the supplement, \emph{Methodology lessons}.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Synthetic data and a small out-of-template benchmark.} All training data is synthetic and template-generated, and the evaluation sets that measure anything real are small. At \nb{T19.benchmark45.n} tickets a single ticket visibly moves accuracy: the Wilson interval on Tier-2's \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac} runs from \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@ci}, and the conformal noise band at $\alpha=\nb{T7.alpha@r2}$ is $\pm$\nb{T7.noise_band_2sd@r3}. Differences smaller than that, which include most comparisons between strong methods, cannot be ordered. The benchmark and the deployment set were written by Gemini, the family that drafts resolutions and forms one zero-shot arm, and the external corpus we used to test transfer is itself generated. Our findings are therefore established on this corpus and have not been shown to hold or fail on real tickets.

\textbf{No live evaluation, and few human quality labels.} No real ticket stream has passed through the system and no help-desk user has acted on its output, so its effect on resolution time, misrouting cost and user trust is unmeasured, and the drift monitor has no deployment-traffic reference. Resolution quality rests on human labels for only \nb{T15.population.eligible} drafts. We could not scale that with an LLM judge, whose \nb{T14.judge.raw_agreement} raw agreement concealed a Cohen's $\kappa$ of \nb{T14.judge.cohens_kappa@r3}, so how often drafts are grounded is known only within a wide interval (\nb{T14.grounded@ci}).

% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
% ===========================================================================
A triage pipeline's value lies in knowing when not to answer. We built a sequential triage pipeline with two independently calibrated escalation gates: a confidence threshold that decides when a lexical classifier may answer alone, and a retrieval threshold that decides when a language model may draft a fix grounded in past tickets. The retrieval gate decides \nb{T3.baseline.escalation_correct} adversarial tickets correctly against \nb{T3.norag.escalation_correct} without it, while letting \nb{T5.ood_leakage_at_gate@pct1}\% of out-of-domain tickets through. The cascade buys latency rather than accuracy, saving \nb{T3.latency.saving.benchmark45@pct0}\% to \nb{T3.latency.saving.deployment175@pct0}\% of median per-ticket time. A human judged \nb{T14.grounded@frac} of the drafts grounded, and an LLM judge could not replace that label ($\kappa=\nb{T14.judge.cohens_kappa@r3}$). Across coverage guarantees, drift monitoring and classification, one result recurs: \emph{the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint}. Recalibrating on deployment-register tickets moved Tier-1's coverage gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3} with nothing else changed, and a zero-shot model that never saw our corpus was indistinguishable from the classifier trained on it.

Three directions follow from the two limitations. First, deployment in a live help desk, which would give real tickets for recalibrating both gates, a deployment-traffic reference so that drift monitoring can run without false alarms, and a direct measure of misrouting cost. Second, a larger human-labelled set of drafts, with labels for context sufficiency as well as draft support, so that resolution quality and any second gate can be measured with narrower intervals and a judge can be audited before it is trusted. Third, a larger out-of-template benchmark on real tickets, which would test whether Finding~1 holds outside our corpus and whether its effect depends on prediction-set size. Code, data and every result file are available at \repourl{} (supplement, \emph{Reproducibility details}).
